summary: For ages 7-9, teach bees and pollination as two linked ideas: the MECHANISM (a bee visits a flower for nectar, pollen sticks to its fuzzy body and rubs off onto the next flower) and the INTERDEPENDENCE (the bee gets food, the plant gets pollinated and can then make seeds and fruit; many of our foods depend on this). The crux children miss is the invisible pollen transfer BETWEEN flowers, so make it visible, distinguish pollination from the later seed/fruit stages, and anchor it to familiar foods like apples and strawberries.
misconceptions: 'Bees make/collect pollen on purpose to pollinate' — pollination is largely an accidental by-product of nectar-seeking.
'Pollen is the same as nectar / a seed' — they are different things with different roles.
'Pollination happens within one flower only' — the key idea is transfer BETWEEN flowers.
'Only bees pollinate' — butterflies, hoverflies, beetles and others pollinate too.
'Bees make honey and that's pollination' — conflating honey production with pollination.

activities.title: Be the bee: carry the pollen flower to flower
steps: Move a bee from one flower to a second flower: at the first flower it drinks nectar and pollen grains cling to its fuzzy body; at the second flower some of that pollen rubs off onto the flower's centre (stigma).

Watch what happens next — the pollinated flower swells and ripens into a fruit (e.g. an apple or strawberry); in this model, flowers that were never visited make no fruit (in real life, unvisited flowers of these plants make little, small or misshapen fruit).
Zoom in to look closely at the pollen grains on the bee's hairs and at the stigma where they land.

Try a 'no pollinators' version: with no bee visiting, the flowers stay unvisited, and in this model none turn to fruit (real plants would make far less fruit); picture a shop shelf with far fewer apples and strawberries. Compare this with the version where bees did visit.
Say in your own words what the bee does for the flower, what the flower does for the bee, and why this matters for the food we eat.
activities.insight: For many plants, pollination happens when pollen accidentally rides from one flower to another on a food-seeking bee; this transfer is what lets the plant make seeds and fruit, so the bee and the flower (and we) depend on each other.

activities.title: Hands-on pollen transfer with a flour-dusted 'bee'
steps: Sprinkle flour (standing for pollen) on the centre of a first paper 'flower', then let a pipe-cleaner or cotton-wool 'bee' visit it so flour clings to the fuzzy 'bee'.
Touch the 'bee' to a second paper 'flower' and look at the flour (pollen) left behind.
Describe how the pollen got from the first flower to the second without the bee meaning to pollinate the flower.
Discuss which part of this is pollination (the pollen moving between flowers), and what comes after it (seeds, then fruit).
activities.insight: Pollen transfer is accidental — it sticks to and rubs off a fuzzy visitor — and it is a separate, earlier step from seed formation and fruit growth.

activities.title: Label the flower and explain why it matters
steps: On a labelled flower-and-bee scene, identify nectar, pollen and stigma and say what each does.
Reveal a 'why it matters' note linking the flower to foods we eat (apples, strawberries, tomatoes).
In your own words, connect each part to its role in the pollination story.
activities.insight: Knowing the named parts (nectar as the bee's food, pollen as what transfers, stigma as where it lands) supports telling the full pollination-to-food story.

activities.title: Order the steps and explore pollinator variety
steps: Put the pollination steps in order: bee visits flower for nectar → pollen sticks to bee → bee visits next flower → pollen rubs off → flower makes seeds → fruit grows.

Look at several pollinators (bees, butterflies, hoverflies, beetles) and work out which insects can visit a given crop, noticing that the SAME crop is often visited by more than one kind — bees are not the only ones, so there is no single exclusive partner.
Answer: what would happen to a garden or orchard if the pollinating insects vanished, and why?
activities.insight: Pollination is a sequence that leads to seeds and fruit, carried out by several kinds of insect, and losing pollinators would reduce the fruit and vegetables we grow.

activities.title: A day in the life of a bee: tell the story
steps: Take the role of a bee and tell or write a short account of visiting flowers: why you go (nectar), what sticks to you, and what you leave behind at the next flower.
Explain 'the deal' between the bee and the plant — what each one gets.
Finish by saying what would happen to the plants, and to our food, if bees like you stopped visiting.
activities.insight: Narrating the bee's visit from its own point of view consolidates both the accidental mechanism and the mutual benefit.

checkQuestion: A bee lands on a flower to drink its sweet nectar, then flies to another flower. Someone says: 'The bee is just getting food — it doesn't do anything for the flower.' Is that right? Tell me what the bee does for the flower without meaning to, and why that matters for the apples and strawberries we eat.
checkAnswer: It's not right — the bee does something important for the flower even though it only came for nectar. Yellow pollen sticks to the bee's furry body, and when it flies to the next flower some pollen rubs off onto it. That is pollination, and it lets the flower make seeds and fruit. Many fruits and vegetables (apples, strawberries) need bees or other insects to pollinate them, so without pollinators we would have far less of these foods.
